summary: Mobility is stabilising near pre‑pandemic levels with the MF‑Index at 72 and PT ridership recovering to about 86% of 2019 volumes. However, real fuel savings are negligible and high‑mobility sectors remain exposed, signalling the need for targeted policy tweaks.

signals.detail: The theoretical ceiling of 35.7 M L/week is far from being realised; only 334 k L were actually saved in the first week, representing ~1 % of the modelled target, indicating negligible real‑world fuel savings.

Daily PT trips of 1.24 M translate to ~450 M trips annually, about 86 % of the 2019 level (522 M). Ridership is climbing from the 2025 recovery but remains below pre‑pandemic, suggesting moderate progress.

Retail & Services, Logistics and Construction together account for >70 % of mobility risk yet have WFH rates below 15 %, exposing the economy to congestion, emissions and productivity losses if no mitigation is introduced.
WFH adoption varies from 60 % in Public & GLCs to 5 % in Construction, creating unequal exposure to commuting burdens and fuel costs across sectors, highlighting equity gaps in the current mandate.
High fuel prices (RON95 RM4.52/L) could incentivise a shift to PT, but the weak real fuel‑saving outcomes and incomplete ridership recovery limit the momentum, yielding only a modest shift potential.

recommendation: Introduce a tiered PT subsidy that reduces fares by 15 % for workers in high‑mobility sectors and expand dedicated bus lanes to improve reliability. Simultaneously, raise the minimum WFH target for Logistics and Construction to 25 % by end‑2027, backed by tax incentives for remote‑work infrastructure. Set a concrete PT ridership goal of 90 % of 2019 levels (≈470 M trips/year) by 2028 and aim for a verified fuel‑saving of at least 5 % of the theoretical ceiling.
